The '''demography of the Republic of Bulgaria''' is monitored by the [[National Statistical Institute of Bulgaria]]. [[Demographics|Demographic]] features of the population of [[Bulgaria]] include population density, [[Ethnic group|ethnicity]], education level, health of the populace, economic status, [[Religion in Bulgaria|religious affiliations]] and others.

The population of Bulgaria was around 6.4 million in 2024.

In 2023, Bulgaria had a [[Human Development Index]] of 0.845, which corresponds to "very high human development", ranking 55th in the world together with neighbouring Romania,<ref>{{cite book |url=https://hdr.undp.org/content/human-development-report-2025 |title=Human Development Report 2025 – A matter of choice: People and possibilities in the age of AI |date=6 May 2025 |publisher=United Nations Development Programme |isbn= |publication-date=6 May 2025 |pages= |access-date=6 May 2025 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20250506064128/https://hdr.undp.org/content/human-development-report-2025 |archive-date=6 May 2025}}</ref> was designated as a "[[World Bank high-income economy|High-income economy]]" by the World Bank, with a [[List of countries by GNI (nominal) per capita|GNI per capita]] of $15,320, as of 2024,<ref>{{Cite web |title=World Bank country classifications by income level for FY26 |url=https://blogs.worldbank.org/en/opendata/understanding-country-income--world-bank-group-income-classifica |access-date=2025-07-01 |website=World Bank Blogs |language=en}}</ref> and was awarded the 38th position in ''[[Newsweek]]''{{'}}s rankings of the world's best countries to live in, measuring health, education, political environment and [[economic dynamism]] in 2010.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.newsweek.com/2010/08/15/interactive-infographic-of-the-worlds-best-countries.html |title=Interactive Infographic of the World's Best Countries |publisher=Newsweek.com |date=15 August 2010 |access-date=24 July 2011 |archive-date=28 July 2011 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110728092003/http://www.newsweek.com/2010/08/15/interactive-infographic-of-the-worlds-best-countries.html |url-status=dead }}</ref>

Various estimates have put Bulgaria's medieval population at 1.1 million in 700 AD and 2.6 million in 1365.<ref>{{cite journal|title=The population of Bulgaria during the Middle Ages (seventh to fourteenth centuries)|date=2014-01-24 |pmid=12280532 |volume=4 |issue= 2|pages=3–11 |journal=Naselenie | last1 = Arkadiev | first1 = D}}</ref> At the 2011 census, the population inhabiting Bulgaria was 7,364,570 in total, but the 2021 census calculated that the population had declined to 6.5 million.<ref name="Census2011final">{{cite web|url=https://www.nsi.bg/census2011/PDOCS2/Census2011final_en.pdf|title=Census 2011|website=Nsi.bg|access-date=2017-08-24}}</ref><ref name="auto">{{Cite web |date= |title=НАСЕЛЕНИЕ КЪМ 7 СЕПТЕМВРИ 2021 ГОДИНА |url=https://nsi.bg/sites/default/files/files/pressreleases/Census2021_population.pdf |access-date=2023-05-11 |website=nsi.bg}}</ref> The peak was in 1989, the year when the borders opened after a half of a century of communist regime, when the population numbered 9,009,018.

==Vital statistics==

===Vital Statistics 1875 to 1899===
The [[total fertility rate]] is the number of children born per woman. It is based on fairly good data for the entire period. Sources: [[Our World in Data]] and [[Gapminder Foundation]].<ref name="ourworldindata.org">{{citation|url=https://ourworldindata.org/grapher/children-born-per-woman?year=1850&country=BGR|title=Total Fertility Rate around the world over the last centuries|author=Max Roser|date=2014|work=[[Our World in Data]], [[Gapminder Foundation]]}}</ref>

Notable events in Bulgarian demography:

* 1912–1913 – [[Second Balkan War|Balkan Wars]] 
* 1915–1918 – [[World War I|First World War]]
* 1989–1990 – [[People's Republic of Bulgaria#End of the People's Republic|End of the People's Republic]] and [[1989 expulsion of Turks from Bulgaria]]
* 2020–2023 – [[COVID-19 pandemic in Bulgaria|COVID-19 pandemic]]

== Birth rates and fertility ==

===Historical birth and fertility rates===
The first reliable data about fertility and natural increase rates in the Bulgarian lands date back to the mid-1800s.

According to Turkish statistician [[Kemal Karpat]], Non-Muslims, Bulgarians included, in the [[Ottoman Empire]] received a remarkable boost in fertility in the early 1830s. Their average growth rate climbed up to 2% per year, compared to zero among Muslims, who suffered from demographic stagnation.<ref name=KKarpat1>{{cite book|last1=Karpat |first1=K.H. |title=Ottoman population, 1830–1914: demographic and social characteristics |publisher=University of Wisconsin Press |location=Madison, Wis |year=1985 | url=https://www.academia.edu/27913581 | pages=70|quote=The assessment of fertility rates is an absolute necessity for the understanding of the growth rate of the Ottoman population. It is generally assumed that during the first thirtv years of the nineteenth century the Ottoman population decreased, beginning to increase again after 1850. This assumption is one-sided and only partly true, for it ignores the differences in growth rates between Muslim and non-Muslim groups. The non-Muslim population actually grew at a fairly fast rate after the 1830s—probably 2 percent annually; the Muslim population declined or remained the same in number. There are indications, however, that fertility rates among the Muslims began to increase after 1850. The causes of the disproportionate fertility rates among the two groups are to be found in the special economic and social conditions which favored non-Muslims and penalized the Muslims, especially Turks. Male Turks spent their peak reproductive years in military service and were unable to marry and settle down to take advantage of economic opportunities. Then, when in the nineteenth century the Ottoman state was exposed to the influence of the European capitalist economy and to intensified internal and international trade, several non-Muslim groups became the early recipients of the economic benefits—and the promoters as well—of the new economic system. }}</ref>

The same trend continued well after Bulgaria's Liberation from Ottoman rule in 1878.<ref name="Godishnik">{{cite journal|journal=Статистически годишник на Българското Царство|publisher=National Statistical Institute|year=1915|language=bg, fr|location=Sofia|title=Статистически годишник на Българското Царство за 1912 г.|trans-title=Statistical Almanac of the Tsardom of Bulgaria for 1912|pages=75–77, 105|url=https://www.nsi.bg/statlib/bg/lister.php?iid=DO-010000465&page=1}}</ref> Until the early 1890s, Muslim birth rates in Bulgaria hesitated in the low 20s, dwarfed by rates of + 40‰ among Orthodox Christians, while natural increase rates hovered around zero.<ref name="Godishnik"/> The ongoing Muslim demographic crisis and the heavy migration to Turkey were the two primary reasons for the rapid decrease in Bulgaria's Muslim and Turkish population between 1880 and 1910, from 28.7% in 1880 to 13.8% in 1910 for Muslims and from 26.2% to 10.7% for Turks.

Muslim birth and natural increase rates started climbing slowly from the late 1890s but only surpassed Orthodox ones in 1924. Nevertheless, it was not the Eastern Orthodox but rather Bulgaria's [[Catholic Church in Bulgaria|Roman Catholics]] that had the highest birth rate during the period, though usually offset by very high mortality rates.

<div style="text-align: center;">'''Average Number of Births & Deaths, Average Birth Rate, Death Rate and Rate of Natural Increase in the Principality of Bulgaria by Period and Confession'''<ref name="Godishnik"/><ref name="Godishnik1930">{{cite journal|journal=Статистически годишник на Българското Царство|publisher=National Statistical Institute|year=1930|language=bg, fr|location=Sofia|title=Статистически годишник на Българското Царство за 1929–1930 г.|trans-title=Statistical Almanac of the Tsardom of Bulgaria for 1929–1930|pages=61, 89|url=https://www.nsi.bg/statlib/bg/lister.php?iid=DO-010000839&page=1}}</ref><ref name="Godishnik1934">{{cite journal|journal=Статистически годишник на Българското Царство|publisher=National Statistical Institute|year=1930|language=bg, fr|location=Sofia|title=Статистически годишник на Българското Царство за 1934 г.|trans-title=Statistical Almanac of the Tsardom of Bulgaria for 1934|pages=53, 64|url=https://www.nsi.bg/statlib/bg/lister.php?iid=DO-010001024&page=1}}</ref></div>

In the 1930s and 1940s, ethnic Bulgarians completed stage 2 of their [[demographic transition]], and crude birth rate among them fell to a mere 23.3‰ by 1946, or twice as low as the birth rate of Bulgaria's two largest minorities, [[Turks in Bulgaria|Turks]] (40.9‰) and [[Romani people in Bulgaria|Roma]] (47.2‰).<ref name=Ilieva>{{cite journal|journal=Проблеми на географията|volume=1-2|year=2011|location=Sofia|publisher=Bulgarian Academy of Sciences|last=Ilieva|first=Nadezhda|title=Промени в локализацията на ромската етническа група в България|trans-title=Problems in the Localisation of Romani in Bulgaria|pages=3|url=https://geoproblems.eu/wp-content/uploads/2016/02/2011_12/4_ilieva.pdf }}</ref> At the same time, due to higher mortality, the rate of natural increase among Bulgarian Turks was almost identical to that among ethnic Bulgarians (12.1‰ vs. 11.1‰), while the rate among the Romani was twice as high (23.1‰).<ref name=Ilieva/>

===Present-day===

A total of 64,984 live births were recorded in Bulgaria in 2016, giving the country a crude birth rate of 9.1‰.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.nsi.bg/en/content/6623/live-births-districts-municipalities-and-sex|title=Live births by districts, municipalities and sex – National statistical institute|website=www.nsi.bg|access-date=14 March 2018|archive-date=15 March 2018|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180315133635/http://www.nsi.bg/en/content/6623/live-births-districts-municipalities-and-sex|url-status=dead}}</ref>

Bulgaria has a low [[total fertility rate]] of 1.58 children per woman (according to the 2021 Census). This is up significantly from the late 1990s, but still below replacement and not enough to prevent further population decline, especially with emigration. Provinces with large Roma populations (for example [[Sliven Province|Sliven]], [[Montana Province|Montana]] and [[Yambol Province|Yambol]]) tend to have higher fertility rates (and higher death rates) compared to other areas, whereas Turkish fertility is similar to the Bulgarian majority.<ref>{{cite news|title=Bulgaria Writes New Chapter In Long Story Of Demographic Decline|url=https://balkaninsight.com/2020/07/09/bulgaria-writes-new-chapter-in-long-story-of-demographic-decline/|date=9 July 2020|access-date=28 October 2020|first=Timothy|last=Judah|newspaper=The Economist|publisher=[[Balkan Insight]]}}</ref> The average number of (live births) children in 2021 was 1.47 for all women (aged 12 or more), ranging from 0.04 children for women between the ages of 12-19 to 1.92 children per women between the ages of 70–79. The distribution by ethnicity shows that only among women who identify themselves as belonging to the Roma ethnic group, the average number of children is sufficient for simple reproduction – 2.25 children, mainly because of the significantly younger age structure and low educational level of this group, followed by the Turkish ethnic group with 1.79 children and 1.41 children for women who self-identified as belonging to the Bulgarian ethnic.<ref>{{cite news|title= NSI – Birth rate, final data|url=https://www.nsi.bg/sites/default/files/files/pressreleases/Census2021-Fertility_en.pdf|date=2021|access-date=22 October 2022|publisher=[[National Statistical Institute (Bulgaria)]]}}</ref> The distribution of the average number of live births by religion changes from 1.83 children for Muslim women and 1.82 children for Protestant women, followed by 'other Christian' (1.63), Eastern Orthodox (1.43), Catholic (1.36), Jewish (1.27) and Armenian Apostolic (1.26). Women without religion had an average number of 1.40 children.

=== Regional differences ===

As of 2022, the municipality of [[Tvarditsa Municipality|Tvarditsa]] has the highest crude birth rate in the country, at 18.4‰, followed by the municipalities of [[Yablanitsa Municipality|Yablanitsa]] (17.9‰) and [[Nikolaevo|Nikolaevo Municipality]] (17.2‰). All these municipalities have relatively large [[Romani people in Bulgaria|Romani]] populations.

=== Teenage pregnancy ===

Bulgaria has one of the highest share of teenage pregnancy in Europe. Nevertheless, this number declined rapidly between 1995 and 2010, until it stabilized at around 10%.

=== Sex ratio ===
Of the total 7,364,570 as of 2011, 3,586,571 are [[male]]s and 3,777,999 are [[female]]s, or there are 1,053 women for every 1,000 men.

== Demographic policies ==

The progressive decrease of the Bulgarian population is hindering economic growth and welfare improvement, and the management measures taken to mitigate the negative consequences do not address the essence of the problem. The Government implemented a program for the period 2017–2021, the first one aimed at reversing this trend. The program identifies the priority means for achieving this goal: measures to increase the birth rate, reduce youth emigration, and build up regulatory and institutional capacity to implement a modern immigration policy tailored to the needs of Bulgarian business.<ref>L. Ivanov. [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/319967867_Demographic_priorities_and_goals_of_the_Government_Program_2017-2021_in_Bulgarian_English_translation Demographic priorities and goals of the Government Program 2017–2021.] Presentation at the round table ''Demographic Policies and Labour Mobility'' organized by the Ministry of Labour and Social Policy, and the State Agency for the Bulgarians Abroad. Sofia, 19 September 2017. 4 pp.</ref><ref>L. Ivanov. [https://www.researchgate.net/publication/321330880_Measures_to_solve_demographic_problems Measures to solve demographic problems.] ''Business Club Magazine''. Issue 11, 2017. pp. 18–20. {{ISSN|2367-623X}} (in Bulgarian and English)</ref>

| colspan="27" |{{smalldiv|1=<sup>'''1'''</sup> According to x files of the state, the number of the Romani was reduced by 25,000 in 1956.<ref name="NUMBER OF ROMA">{{cite book|last1=Ilieva|first1=Nadezhda|url=https://geoproblems.eu/wp-content/uploads/2016/01/2012_34/5_ilieva.pdf|title=NUMBER OF ROMA ETHNIC GROUP IN BULGARIA FROM THE LIBERATION TO THE BEGINNING OF THE 21ST CENTURY (BASED ON REGULAR CENSUSES) (Part 1)|date=2012|location=Bulgarian Academy of Sciences|pages=74–75}}</ref>

<sup>'''2'''</sup> In the 1946 census, the population of Pirin Macedonia was forced to list as ethnic Macedonians by the [[People's Republic of Bulgaria|Communist government]] in preparation of a planned federation between the [[People's Republic of Bulgaria]] and [[Socialist Yugoslavia]], with "United Macedonia" as the connecting piece. The deal fell through after [[Tito-Stalin split]] in 1948. Since Stalin's death in 1953, Bulgaria started changing its policy on the Macedonians.<ref name="Rotschild">{{cite book | last=v | first=Joseph | title=The Communist Party of Bulgaria; Origins and Development, 1883–1936 | publisher=[[Columbia University Press]] | page=126 }}</ref><ref name="Cook">{{cite book | last=A. Cook | first=Bernard | title=Europe Since 1945: An Encyclopedia | publisher=[[Taylor & Francis]] | year=2001 | page=810 | isbn=978-0-8153-4058-4 }}</ref>

<sup>'''3'''</sup> In the 1956 census, the Bulgarian authorities favored Bulgarian self-identification of the population in Pirin Macedonia. However, despite presence of pressures by the regime to declare as Bulgarians, the majority of the population still declared themselves as Macedonian.<ref>{{cite book|first=Tchavdar|last=Marinov|year=2010|title=La Question Macédonienne de 1944 à nos jours : Communisme et nationalism dans les Balkans|publisher=Éditions L’Harmattan|page=87}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Detrez |first=Raymond|title=The A to Z of Bulgaria |publisher=Scarecrow Press|year=2010 |isbn=9780810872028 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_to_Z_of_Bulgaria/LdRXAAAAYAAJ|page=277|quote=In the 1956 census, however, when they were pressured to declare themselves Bulgarians, 178,862 people still signed up as Macedonians.}}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last=Pettifer |first=James |title=Greece and the New Balkans: Themes and Histories |publisher=[[Signal Books]]|location=Oxford| year=2026 |isbn=9780722361757|quote=In the 1956 census, 187,000 people declared themselves to be Macedonians, despite political pressure from the regime.}}</ref> After 1958, the Bulgarian authorities started openly denying the existence of a Macedonian minority in the country.

<sup>'''4'''</sup> Note that the distinction between [[Sarakatsani]] and Greeks, and between Vlachs and both Aromanians and Romanians, is fluid. Sarakatsani were counted as Greeks in the 1900, 1920, 1926, 1934, and 1965 censuses.}}

The 2001 census defines an ethnic group as a "community of people, related to each other by origin and language, and close to each other by mode of life and culture"; and one's mother tongue as "the language a person speaks best and usually uses for communication in the family (household)".<ref name="culturalpolicies.net">{{cite web |author=Cultural Policies and Trends in Europe |title=Population by ethnic group and mother tongue, 2001 |url=http://www.culturalpolicies.net/web/bulgaria.php?aid=421 |access-date=2 December 2008 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150923211849/http://www.culturalpolicies.net/web/bulgaria.php?aid=421 |archive-date=23 September 2015 |url-status=dead }}</ref>
According to the 2011 census, among the Bulgarians 99.4% indicate Bulgarian as a mother tongue, 0.3% – Turkish/Balkan gagauz, 0.1% – Roma and 0.1% others; among Turks 96.6% have pointed the Turkish/Balkan Gagauz as a mother tongue and 3.2% – Bulgarian; among the Roma 85% indicate Roma language as a mother tongue, 7.5% – Bulgarian, 6.7% – Turkish/Balkan gagauz and 0.6% – Romanian.

== Religion ==
{{Main|Religion in Bulgaria}}

Bulgaria's traditional religion according to the constitution is the [[Bulgarian Orthodox Church|Orthodox Christianity]], while Bulgaria is a [[secular state]] too. Since the last two censuses (2001 and 2011) provide widely divergent results, they are both shown in the table below. It is noteworthy that over a fifth of the population chose not to respond to this question in the 2011 census.

==Migration==
{{main|Immigration to Bulgaria}}

===Historical migration===
The first censuses of the [[Principality of Bulgaria]] and the autonomous province of [[Eastern Rumelia]] in 1880 recorded 31,786 and 17,970 Bulgarian refugees from [[Macedonia (region)|Macedonia]] and [[Adrianople Vilayet|Ottoman Thrace]], respectively, who accounted for 1.38% of the population of the Principality an 2.20% of the population of the autonomous province, respectively.<ref name="1881 Census">{{Citation|title=Общи резултати от преброяването на населението на 1 януарий 1881 г.|trans-title=General Results of the Census of the Population of 1 January 1881|url=https://www.nsi.bg/statlib/bg/lister.php?iid=DO-010000007&page=16|pages=16–17|publisher=National Statistical Institute|language=bg}}</ref><ref name="Balev">{{cite web | first1=Ivan| last1=Balev |url=https://www.nsi.bg/spisaniestatistika/page/download.php?articleID=78 | trans-title=Unrecognised Censuses in the History of Bulgarian Statistics|title=НЕПРИЗНАТИТЕ" ПРЕБРОЯВАНИЯ В ИСТОРИЯТА НА БЪЛГАРСКАТА СТАТИСТИКА | language=bg | date=2017 | pages=10–11}}</ref><ref name="Thrace">{{Cite book| title=Сборник Тракия, т. 1|trans-title=Collection Thrace |volume=I| url=https://macedonia.kroraina.com/tr/1/trakij_1_2001_4.htm |date=2001|pages=51|publisher=Thracian Scientific Institute, [[Haskovo]] Branch|language=bg}}</ref> The census of the Principality also counted a total of 37,635 people, or 1.88% of the population, born in a country other than the [[Ottoman Empire]], mostly Bulgarians from [[Bulgarians in Romania|Romania]], [[Northern Dobruja]] and [[Bessarabian Bulgarians|Bessarabia]].<ref name="1881 Census"/> By 1887, when the first joint census of the Principality and the autonomous province was conducted following their peaceful [[Bulgarian unification|unification]] in 1885, the number of the refugees from the Ottoman Empire had grown to 54,462 people, or 1.73% of the population, while the rest of the foreign-born population had fallen to 31,637 people, 9,831 of whom born in the [[Russian Empire]], 11,843 in [[Romania]], 2,690 in [[Serbia]] and 7,273 elsewhere.<ref name="1887 Census">{{Citation|title=Общи резултати от преброяването на населението на 1 януарий 1887 г.|trans-title=General Results of the Census of the Population of 1 January 1888|date=1890|url=https://www.nsi.bg/statlib/bg/lister.php?iid=DO-010000078&page=16|pages=16–17|publisher=National Statistical Institute|language=bg}}</ref>

According to the 1910 census, 300,000 or almost 10% of the ethnic Bulgarians were born in another Bulgarian municipality than the one they were enumerated in. The same data shows that the foreign-born ethnic Bulgarians numbered 78,000, or 2% of them, most numerous of whom were the 61,000 [[Ottoman Empire|Ottoman]]-born, 9,000 Romanian-born and by less than 2,000 [[Austro-Hungarian Empire|Austro-Hungarian]], Serbian and Russian-born.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://statlib.nsi.bg:8181/en/lister.php?iid=DO-010000566&page=62|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170206185503/http://statlib.nsi.bg:8181/en/lister.php?iid=DO-010000566&page=62|url-status=dead|archive-date=6 February 2017|title=iLib – Lister|date=6 February 2017|access-date=15 October 2017}}</ref> By the 1926 census, there had been 253,000 refugees with granted households and land or citizenship but with many more in towns of uncertain number. 35% came from [[Eastern Thrace]], 30% came from [[Macedonia (Greece)|Greek Macedonia]], another 18% from [[Western Thrace]], 8% from [[Dobruja]], 4% from the [[Western Outlands]], 3% from [[Asia Minor]], and 2% from [[North Macedonia]]. They constituted 6% of the country's population. In 1940, 70,000 Bulgarians [[Population exchange between Bulgaria and Romania|were exchanged]] from [[Northern Dobruja]]. The total number of refugees in 1878–1940 is estimated at between 700,000 and 1,200,000.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://docplayer.net/35763499-Communities-identities-and-migrations-in-southeast-europe.html|title=Communities, Identities and Migrations in Southeast Europe – PDF|website=docplayer.net|access-date=24 August 2017}}</ref> [[Exodus of Turks from Bulgaria (1950–1951)|In 1950–1951, around 150,000 Turks left Bulgaria]] for Turkey, and [[Big Excursion|again in 1989]].

===Current  migration===
According to the 2011 census [[Russia]]n citizens are the most numerous foreigners – 11 991, followed by 8 444 EU citizens (UK – 2 605, Greece – 1 253, Germany – 848, Poland – 819 and Italy – 456), citizens of [[Ukraine]] – 3 064, [[North Macedonia]] – 1 091, [[Moldova]] – 893 and [[Serbia]] – 569. 22.8% of them are from Asia, mostly from Turkey. Those with dual Bulgarian and other citizenship were 22 152, or 0.3% of the population. Of them persons with Bulgarian and Russian citizenship were 5 257 (23.7%), followed by persons with Bulgarian and Turkish citizenship – 4 282 (19.3%), Bulgarian and citizenship of the USA – 1 725 (7.8%). There are at least 17,527 [[Refugees of the Syrian Civil War]] with applications in Bulgaria. In 2001–2015 185,447 people applied for Bulgarian citizenship and 116,222 were provided with. 113,647 were granted on grounds of proven Bulgarian ancestry, including 59,968 North Macedonia citizens. 29,218 were [[Moldova]]n citizens, 5930 Ukrainians, 5374 Serbians, 5194 Russians, 3840 Israeli, 2192 Albanians, 692 Turks and others.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://dariknews.bg/regioni/blagoevgrad/59-968-makedonci-dokazali-bylgarski-proizhod-1452177|title=59 968 македонци доказали български произход – Благоевград |website=DarikNews.bg|date=11 June 2015 |access-date=24 August 2017}}</ref> In 2016, 12,880 foreigners were naturalized, including 6196 Macedonians.<ref>{{cite web|title=Президент на Република България|url=https://www.president.bg/cat107/Godishni-dokladi-grajdanstvo/|website=President.bg|access-date=2017-08-24}}</ref>

== Age structure ==
:0–14 years: {{decrease}} 13.2%
:15–65 years: {{increase}} 68.3%
:65 years and over: {{negative increase}} 18.5% (Census 2011)<ref name=Census2011final />
At the 2011 census, the largest cohort of those self-identified as [[Romani people|Romani]] was the 0–9 years cohort, which accounted for 20.8% of all Romani. The same age cohort accounted for 10.2% of the [[Turkish people|Turks]] and 7.2% of the [[Bulgarians]].<ref name="censusresults.nsi.bg"/> At the 2021 census, the 0–9 years cohort amongst the Romani was second largest after the 10–19 years one and represented 17.0% of all Romani.<ref name=Infostat5>{{cite web |website=Инфостат|url=https://infostat.nsi.bg/infostat/pages/reports/result.jsf?x_2=2139|title=Population by Ethnic Group and Age as of 07.09.2021}}</ref> The corresponding percentages for ethnic Bulgarians and ethnic Turks stood at 7.7% and 8.8%, respectively.

Bulgarian children constitute the majority of all children in 23 out of 28 provinces. They constitute more than ninety percent of all children in two provinces: [[Sofia|Sofia (city)]] (92%) and [[Pernik Province]] (90%).

Turkish children constitute the majority in [[Kardzhali Province]] (68% of self-declared) and [[Razgrad Province]] (50% of self-declared); they also constitute the largest group of all children in [[Silistra Province]] (43%).

Roma children constitute 12% of all children in Bulgaria and more than a quarter in three provinces: [[Montana Province|Montana]] (29%), [[Sliven Province|Sliven]] (28%) and [[Yambol Province|Yambol]] (27%).

Bulgaria is ageing rapidly, especially in some remote rural areas.

The ageing of the population leads to an increase of the median age. The median age is 43.6 as of 2017, up from 40.4 years in 2001.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nsi.bg/sites/default/files/files/pressreleases/Population2017_en_R5PBSJP.pdf |title=POPULATION AND DEMOGRAPHIC PROCESSES IN 2017 |access-date=2018-05-05}}</ref>

== Education ==
{{main|Education in Bulgaria}}
{{multiple image |total_width=300 |align=left |image1=Cocencms202-2 (L).png |caption1=Map of Romani students in schools in Bulgaria |image2=Cocencms202-2 (R).png |caption2=Chart of completed degrees by ethnic groups in Bulgaria}}

Over 98% of the population is literate, the males being more literate than the females.

According to the 2011 census, about 112,778 people aged nine or more are [[illiterate]]. There are considerable differences in the share of illiterate persons amongst the three main ethnic groups. Amongst the Bulgarian ethnic group the share of illiterate is 0.5%, amongst the Turkish – 4.7% and amongst the Roma ethnic group – 11.8%.<ref>[https://www.nsi.bg/census2011/PDOCS2/Census2011final_en.pdf 2011 census results]</ref> About 81 thousand people aged seven or more never visited school.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://sociobrains.com/website/w1465/file/repository/14_20_Sonya_Ilieva_Predominating_risk_groups_in_Bulgarian_society.pdf |title=Risk report |website=sociobrains.com }}</ref>

== Unemployment ==
[[File:Bulgaria socio-economic map.jpg|left|thumb|upright=0.8|Chart of unemployment and poverty rate by ethnic groups]]

The number of unemployed people declined from 207,000 people (or around 6.2% of the population) in 2017<ref>Unemployed and unemployment rates – national level; statistical regions; districts [http://www.nsi.bg/en/content/6503/unemployed-and-unemployment-rates-national-level-statistical-regions-districts] {{Webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180407183612/http://www.nsi.bg/en/content/6503/unemployed-and-unemployment-rates-national-level-statistical-regions-districts|date=7 April 2018}}</ref> to 156,657 in November 2023. The unemployment rate stood at 4.3 per cent in November 2023 according to [[Eurostat]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://sofiaglobe.com/2024/01/09/eurostat-unemployment-in-bulgaria-in-november-2023-was-4-3/ |date=9 January 2024 |title=Eurostat: Unemployment in Bulgaria in November 2023 was 4.3% }}</ref>

Most unemployed people are aged 15 to 24 years old.

The [[unemployment rate]] in rural areas (around 10.0%) is nearly two times higher than the unemployment rate in urban areas (approximately 5.1%).

[[Vidin Province]] has the highest unemployment rate with almost one fifth of its labour force being unemployed. The provinces of [[Shumen Province|Shumen]] (15.9%), [[Silistra Province|Silistra]] (12.5%) and [[Targovishte Province|Targovishte]] (12.4%) also have very high unemployment rates.

== Other statistics ==

=== Home ownership ===
According to [[Eurostat]], 82.3% per cent of the population live in privately owned and owner-occupied homes, ranking it as 12th [[List of countries by home ownership rate|highest in ownership]] globally.<ref name=":0">{{cite web|url=http://appsso.eurostat.ec.europa.eu/nui/show.do?query=BOOKMARK_DS-057102_QID_684D63DF_UID_-3F171EB0&layout=TIME,C,X,0;GEO,L,Y,0;INCGRP,L,Z,0;HHTYP,L,Z,1;TENURE,L,Z,2;INDICATORS,C,Z,3;&zSelection=DS-057102INDICATORS,OBS_FLAG;DS-057102INCGRP,TOTAL;DS-057102TENURE,OWN;DS-057102HHTYP,TOTAL;&rankName1=HHTYP_1_2_-1_2&rankName2=INDICATORS_1_2_-1_2&rankName3=INCGRP_1_2_-1_2&rankName4=TENURE_1_2_-1_2&rankName5=TIME_1_0_0_0&rankName6=GEO_1_2_0_1&sortR=ASC_0&sortC=ASC_-1_FIRST&rStp=&cStp=&rDCh=&cDCh=&rDM=true&cDM=true&footnes=false&empty=false&wai=false&time_mode=NONE&time_most_recent=false&lang=EN&cfo=%23%23%23%2C%23%23%23.%23%23%23|title=Eurostat – Data Explorer – Distribution of population by tenure status, type of household and income group|publisher=[[Eurostat]]|access-date=23 October 2016}}</ref> It is down from a recent peak of 87.6% in 2008, and has been steadily falling since.<ref name=":0" />

=== Internet penetration ===
The number of Internet users has increased rapidly since 2000—from 430,000 their number grew to 1.55&nbsp;million in 2004, and 3.4&nbsp;million (48 per cent penetration rate) in 2010.<ref>{{cite web |url=http://www.internetworldstats.com/eu/bg.htm |title=Bulgaria Internet Usage Stats and Market Report |publisher=Internetworldstats.com |date=30 June 2010 |access-date=20 December 2011}}</ref> Bulgaria has the third-fastest average Broadband Internet speed in the world after South Korea and Romania with an average speed of 1,611&nbsp;kbit/s.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://sofiaecho.com/2011/09/21/1161236_bulgaria-ranks-third-in-global-internet-speed-survey|title=Bulgaria ranks third in global Internet speed survey|newspaper=[[The Sofia Echo]]|date=21 September 2011|access-date=8 June 2012|archive-date=17 June 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120617201929/http://sofiaecho.com/2011/09/21/1161236_bulgaria-ranks-third-in-global-internet-speed-survey|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.itu.int/ITU-D/ict/facts/2011/material/ICTFactsFigures2011.pdf |title=The World in 2011 – Facts and Figures |date=February 2012 |publisher=[[International Telecommunication Union]] |access-date=27 April 2012}}</ref>

=== Mobile phone adoption ===
Currently there are three active mobile phone operators—[[Mobiltel|A1]], [[Yettel]] and [[Vivacom]], A1 is the largest one with 5.2 million users as of 2010,<ref name="managerblitz">{{cite web|url=http://www.manager.bg/broi-132/menidzhmant/%E2%80%9Cm-tel-blits-s-andreas-mayerhofer|title="М-Тел" блиц с Андреас Майерхофер – списание МЕНИДЖЪР|date=23 April 2012|website=Manager.bg|access-date=24 August 2017|url-status=dead|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120423010908/http://www.manager.bg/broi-132/menidzhmant/%E2%80%9Cm-tel-blits-s-andreas-mayerhofer|archive-date=23 April 2012}}</ref> Yettel has 3,9 million as of 2007 and Vivacom over 1 million{{Citation needed|date=April 2017}}.

=== HIV ===
Bulgaria's [[List of countries by HIV/AIDS adult prevalence rate|HIV rate]] is among the lowest in the world, being 0.1% or 3,800 infected as of 2009.{{Citation needed|date=April 2017}}

== Urbanization ==
{{see also|List of cities and towns in Bulgaria}}

Most Bulgarians (72.5 per cent) reside in urban areas. Approximately one-sixth of them live in Sofia, which has a population exceeding 1,200,000 people.

:Urban population: {{increase}} 5,338,261 or 72.5% of total population (Census 2011)<ref name=Census2011final />
:Rural: 2,026,309 or 27.5%
:Rate of urbanization: −0.3% annual rate of change (2005–10 est.)
